title: NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora
subtitle: Load corpora, clean and normalise raw text, tokenise it with regular expressions, and count, compare and model words in Python with NLTK.
outcomes: Tokenise, normalise and pattern-match raw text with Python strings, Unicode normalisation and regular expressions
Load NLTK's corpora and your own, and compare them with frequency and conditional frequency distributions
Build a simple bigram language model from scratch and evaluate its perplexity on test sentences
Use WordNet's synsets, lexical relations and similarity scores for basic semantic tasks
Write streaming, well-organised NLP scripts with generators, small functions and pytest tests
Compute minimum edit distance for spelling correction and explain how subword tokenisers such as BPE split words
prerequisites: Basic Python: variables, loops, functions, lists and dictionaries, and running a script (Python Programming with PyCharm or Python Foundations for Data Science covers them). No NLP experience is needed. You need Python 3.10 or later with NLTK 3.9 or later and pytest (pip install nltk pytest); each lab gives the exact nltk.download() calls for the corpora it uses, about 25 MB in all.
description:
Every language technology, from a search box to a chat assistant, starts by turning raw text into something a program can count. This course teaches those foundations in Python with NLTK, the toolkit generations of NLP students have learned with. You'll treat text as data (tokens, types and vocabularies), load classic corpora such as Brown and Project Gutenberg as well as your own files, compare genres with conditional frequency distributions, and look up meanings and relations in WordNet.

Then you'll clean real-world text: decode it correctly, normalise Unicode so that 'café' always counts as one word, strip HTML, and reduce words to stems or lemmas, knowing what each step gains and loses. You'll write NLP code that scales and can be trusted, with generators, small pure functions and pytest, and use it to build and test a bigram language model whose perplexity you measure. The last module puts regular expressions to work: groups and lookarounds, tokenisers for messy text, minimum edit distance for spelling correction, and the byte-pair encoding behind modern subword tokenisers. Every module ends with a lab whose starter files and expected output you can check line by line, and the course finishes with a mini-corpus pipeline you build end to end. It prepares you for Statistical NLP: Models, Parsing and Information Retrieval and for Text Representation: From Vectors to Context.

modules.title: Language processing and Python essentials
modules.summary: See text as data a program can count: tokens, types and vocabularies, the Python strings and lists that hold them, a first processing pipeline, and the linguistic ideas every NLP system runs into.

lessons.title: Tokens, types and vocabulary
objectives: Tell tokens from types and count both in a text
Calculate lexical diversity and explain why a text's length affects it
Describe how word frequencies are distributed in real text
key_points: A token is one occurrence of a word, number or punctuation mark in a text; a type is a distinct form. 'the cat saw the dog' has five tokens but four types, because 'the' occurs twice.
A text's vocabulary is its set of types: len(tokens) counts tokens and len(set(tokens)) counts types. Normalisation choices change the answer: with case kept, 'The' and 'the' are two types.

Lexical diversity, or the type-token ratio, is types divided by tokens. It falls as a text grows, because common words keep repeating while new ones appear more slowly, so compare texts of similar length or equal-sized samples.

Word frequencies are very uneven and roughly follow Zipf's law: a word's frequency is about inversely proportional to its rank, so a few function words such as 'the', 'of' and 'and' make up a large share of all tokens.

At the other end, many types occur only once; they're called hapax legomena, or hapaxes. Of the 7,079 lowercased word types in Jane Austen's Emma, as NLTK's Gutenberg corpus tokenises it, 2,739 appear just once.

lessons.title: Python strings and lists for text
objectives: Inspect and change text with string methods, indexing and slicing
Build and filter lists of tokens with comprehensions and sets
key_points: A Python str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters: text[0] is the first character and text[-4:] the last four, and methods such as lower() and replace() return a new string rather than changing the original.

text.split() with no argument splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty strings, but punctuation stays attached, so 'sat.' and 'sat' are different tokens until you strip it, for example with w.strip('.,!?').
str.strip(chars) removes the given characters from both ends only, never from the middle, so "don't" keeps its apostrophe; ' '.join(tokens) turns a list of tokens back into one string.
List comprehensions transform and filter in one line: [w.lower() for w in tokens if w.isalpha()] keeps only the alphabetic tokens, lowercased.

The in operator depends on what's on its right: 'cat' in 'concatenate' is True because it looks for a substring, but 'cat' in ['concatenate'] is False because it checks list membership. Sets give fast membership tests for large vocabularies.

lessons.title: A first text-processing pipeline
objectives: Break a text-processing task into stages: read, normalise, tokenise, filter and count
Explain how each stage's choices change the results
key_points: A pipeline is a sequence of small steps, each working on the previous step's output: read the raw text, normalise it (for example, lowercase it), split it into tokens, filter out what you don't need, then count or analyse what's left.
Open text files with an explicit encoding, open(path, encoding='utf-8'), so the script reads the same characters on every computer whatever the system's default encoding is.

Stop words are frequent function words such as 'the', 'and' and 'of'. Removing them reveals the content words that characterise a text, but the list must match your normalisation (most lists are lowercase), and for some tasks, such as sentiment, words like 'not' matter.

collections.Counter and NLTK's FreqDist, a Counter subclass, count tokens; most_common(5) returns the five most frequent (token, count) pairs, and tied counts keep the order in which their tokens were first seen.
Keep each stage a separate function and leave the raw text untouched, so you can change one decision, such as keeping numbers or case, and rerun the rest to see its effect.

lessons.title: Linguistic ideas behind NLP
objectives: Use basic linguistic terms: morpheme, inflection, derivation, part of speech, syntax and semantics
Recognise ambiguity at different levels of language
key_points: Morphology is the study of word structure. A morpheme is the smallest unit with meaning, so 'unhappiness' has three (un-, happy, -ness); inflection changes a word's grammatical form (walk, walks, walked) while derivation makes a new word (happy, happiness).

Parts of speech group words by how they behave in sentences. Open classes (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) take new members all the time; closed classes (determiners, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions) rarely change and supply most stop words.
Syntax is how words combine into phrases and sentences, semantics is what they mean, and pragmatics is meaning in context: 'Can you pass the salt?' is a request, not a question about ability.

Language is ambiguous at every level: lexical ('bank' as a riverside or a lender), structural ('I saw the man with the telescope': who has the telescope?) and referential ('it' can point to several things).

Habits from English don't carry over: Chinese, Japanese and Thai are written without spaces between words, and languages such as Turkish and Finnish build long words from many morphemes, so splitting on spaces works badly for them.

The Night Ferry

The night ferry left the harbour at nine, and Nora was always on it. She sold tea from a small cart on the lower deck, and she knew most of the passengers by their faces, if not by their names. There was the man with the grey dog, who read the same newspaper every night. There were the two students who argued about music. There was the old woman who knitted a blue scarf that never seemed to grow.

On Tuesday the sea was rough. The ferry rolled, and the tea cart rolled with it. Nora held the cart with one hand and the kettle with the other. "Tea for the brave," she called, and the students laughed, and the man with the grey dog put down his newspaper.

"Is it always like this?" asked a passenger Nora had never seen before. He was young, with a wet coat and a small wooden box under his arm.

"Only when the wind comes from the west," said Nora. "Tea?"

He bought a cup of tea and sat on the bench beside the cart. The box stayed under his arm. Nora tried not to look at it, but it was hard not to look at a box that someone held so carefully.

"It's a clock," he said at last. "My grandmother's clock. It stopped the night she died, and I'm taking it to a man on the island who mends clocks."

"There is a clock man on the island," Nora agreed. "He mended my father's watch. He works slowly, but he works well."

The ferry rolled again. The old woman dropped her knitting, and the blue scarf slid across the deck. The grey dog chased it. The students chased the dog. For a moment the whole lower deck was a game, and even the young man with the box was laughing.

When the scarf was safe and the dog was calm, Nora poured more tea. The wind dropped a little. Through the window they could see the lights of the island, small and yellow, like a row of lanterns on a shelf.

"Will he be able to mend it?" asked the young man.

"I don't know," said Nora. "But he will try. That is what the island is good at. Trying."

The ferry reached the harbour at eleven. The passengers walked down the ramp one by one: the man with the grey dog, the two students, the old woman with her scarf, and the young man with the wooden box. Nora washed the cups and counted the coins. It had been a good night for tea.

Two weeks later the young man was on the ferry again. He did not have the box. He bought a cup of tea and sat on the bench beside the cart, as before.

"Well?" said Nora.

"It works," he said. "The clock man found a broken spring. He said the clock was older than the ferry, older than the harbour, maybe older than the oldest house on the island."

"And now it is ticking again."

"Now it is ticking again. It's on my kitchen wall, and every hour it rings, and every hour I think of her."

Nora smiled and poured herself a cup of tea, which she almost never did. Outside, the sea was calm, and the lights of the island were small and yellow, like a row of lanterns on a shelf.

modules.title: Accessing text corpora and WordNet
modules.summary: Load NLTK's corpora and your own text files, compare categories with conditional frequency distributions and turn bigram counts into probabilities, then use WordNet's synsets and relations to work with meaning.

lessons.title: Corpus readers: Gutenberg, Brown and your own files
objectives: Download NLTK corpora and load them with corpus readers
Read a folder of your own text files as a corpus
key_points: A corpus is a large, structured collection of texts for studying language. nltk.download('brown') fetches a corpus once into an nltk_data folder, and nltk.corpus.brown then loads it lazily, the first time you use it.

Corpus readers share one interface: fileids() lists the files, raw() returns text as a string, words() the tokens and sents() the sentences as lists of tokens, for the whole corpus or for chosen files.

The Brown corpus has about 1.16 million words of 1961 American English in 15 categories, such as news, government and romance, so brown.words(categories='news') lets you compare genres; tagged_words() pairs each token with its part-of-speech tag.

PlaintextCorpusReader(folder, r'.*\.txt') turns your own folder of text files into a corpus with the same methods; its words() splits text with WordPunctTokenizer, and its sents() needs the punkt_tab sentence model.
Recent NLTK releases only let corpus readers open folders on NLTK's data path, so if PlaintextCorpusReader raises PermissionError ('Unauthorized path'), call nltk.data.path.append(folder) first.

lessons.title: Conditional frequency distributions and bigram probabilities
objectives: Count words with FreqDist and compare categories with ConditionalFreqDist
Turn bigram counts into conditional probabilities
key_points: FreqDist counts samples: fd['ferry'] is a count, fd.N() the total number of tokens, fd.freq('ferry') the relative frequency and fd.hapaxes() the words seen once.

A ConditionalFreqDist keeps one FreqDist per condition and is built from (condition, sample) pairs, such as (genre, word) for every word in several Brown categories; cfd['romance']['she'] is then a count within one condition.

cfd.tabulate(conditions=..., samples=...) prints a table of counts that makes differences easy to see: in Brown, 'she' occurs 728 times in romance but once in government. Compare relative frequencies, not raw counts, when the categories differ in size.

Built from bigrams, pairs of neighbouring words, a ConditionalFreqDist records which words follow each word, and dividing by the condition's total gives the maximum likelihood estimate P(word | previous) = count(previous, word) / count(previous).

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland 'mock' is always followed by 'turtle', so P(turtle | mock) = 1. Always choosing the likeliest next word soon loops ('the queen and the queen and ...'), an early sign that generating text needs sampling.

lessons.title: WordNet: synsets, lemmas and senses
objectives: Look up a word's senses, definitions and examples in WordNet
Tell synsets from lemmas
key_points: WordNet is a large lexical database of English that groups nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs into synsets: sets of synonyms that express one concept, each with a short definition and often example sentences. NLTK's copy is WordNet 3.0, fetched with nltk.download('wordnet').
wn.synsets('bank') returns every synset containing the word, 18 noun and verb senses in all. A synset name such as bank.n.01 reads as a word, a part of speech and a sense number.

A synset's lemmas are its member words: car.n.01 has the lemma names car, auto, automobile, machine and motorcar. A lemma is a word in one sense, so 'bank' in bank.n.01 (sloping land) and 'bank' in depository_financial_institution.n.01 are different lemmas.
Filter by part of speech, as in wn.synsets('run', pos=wn.VERB), which returns 41 verb senses; function words such as 'the' and 'of' aren't in WordNet at all.
Senses are numbered roughly from most to least frequent in a sense-tagged corpus, so the first synset is a sensible default when nothing else is known, though it's often the wrong sense.

lessons.title: Lexical relations and similarity
objectives: Navigate hypernyms, hyponyms, meronyms, holonyms and antonyms
Measure how closely two senses are related with path similarity
key_points: Hypernyms are more general concepts and hyponyms more specific ones. dog.n.01 has two hypernyms, canine.n.02 and domestic_animal.n.01, and following hypernyms upwards always ends at entity.n.01, the root of the noun hierarchy.
Meronyms are parts and holonyms are wholes: tree.n.01's part meronyms include trunk, limb and crown, its substance meronyms are heartwood and sapwood, and its member holonym is forest.
Antonyms link lemmas rather than synsets: wn.lemma('good.a.01.good').antonyms() returns the lemma bad.a.01.bad.

path_similarity scores two synsets from the shortest path between them in the hypernym hierarchy, 1 for the same synset and falling towards 0: dog and wolf score 0.333, dog and cat 0.2 (they meet at carnivore.n.01) and dog and car about 0.077.

Relations like these help expand search queries with synonyms or group words by concept, but WordNet is built by hand, so it misses new words and slang and covers English far better than other languages.

modules.title: Processing raw text and normalisation
modules.summary: Turn messy real-world text into clean tokens: decode bytes correctly, normalise Unicode, extract text from HTML, and reduce words to stems or lemmas, knowing what each step changes.

lessons.title: Encodings and Unicode normalisation
objectives: Decode text files with the right encoding and recognise mojibake
Normalise Unicode with NFC, NFKC and casefold, and say what each changes
key_points: Files store bytes and an encoding maps them to characters. Decode with the encoding the text was written in, usually UTF-8, because the wrong one produces mojibake: 'café' saved as UTF-8 but read as Latin-1 comes out as 'cafÃ©'.

The same visible text can be made of different code points: 'é' can be one precomposed character (U+00E9) or 'e' followed by a combining acute accent (U+0301), so 'café' written both ways looks identical but compares unequal, with lengths 4 and 5.

unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s) composes characters and 'NFD' decomposes them. Normalise all text to one form, usually NFC, before comparing, counting or tokenising it: the regex \w+ splits the decomposed form and drops the accent.

The compatibility forms NFKC and NFKD also fold look-alike variants: the ligature 'ﬁ' becomes 'fi' and full-width '２０２４' becomes '2024'. They can erase real distinctions too, such as superscript '²' becoming '2', so use them deliberately.

str.casefold() is a stronger lower() for caseless matching: 'Straße'.lower() keeps the 'ß' but casefold() gives 'strasse'. Stripping accents (decompose, then drop combining marks) helps fuzzy search but changes meaning: Spanish 'papá' (dad) becomes 'papa' (potato).

lessons.title: Text from the web: HTML, entities and boilerplate
objectives: Extract readable text from an HTML page, skipping scripts, styles and boilerplate
Clean up entities, whitespace and typographic punctuation
key_points: Web pages mix the text you want with markup, scripts, styles and boilerplate such as menus and footers. Extract text with an HTML parser rather than regular expressions, which break on nested, broken or unusual markup.

Python's html.parser.HTMLParser calls your handle_starttag, handle_endtag and handle_data methods as it reads, so a small subclass can skip everything inside <script>, <style>, <nav> and <footer>; libraries such as Beautiful Soup do the same with less code.

HTML entities encode characters: & is &, é is é, ’ is a curly apostrophe and   a no-break space (U+00A0). HTMLParser decodes them in text by default (convert_charrefs=True), and html.unescape() decodes them anywhere else.
Collapse whitespace with re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text); in Python 3, \s in a str pattern also matches Unicode whitespace such as the no-break space.

Typographic characters look like ASCII but aren't: 'don’t' with a curly apostrophe and "don't" are different strings to a tokeniser. Map curly quotes to straight ones, or allow both in your patterns, before tokenising.

lessons.title: Stemming algorithms
objectives: Explain how rule-based stemmers strip suffixes
Compare the Porter, Snowball and Lancaster stemmers and their typical errors
key_points: A stemmer cuts affixes off with rules so that related forms share a stem: Porter turns 'studies' and 'studying' into 'studi'. Stems needn't be real words; they only need to match each other.

The Porter stemmer (1980) applies several steps of suffix rules, each with conditions on the stem that remains. SnowballStemmer('english') implements its revised successor, often called Porter2, and Snowball has stemmers for many other languages, such as Spanish, Arabic and Swedish.
The Lancaster stemmer is the most aggressive of the three: it turns 'organization' into 'org' and 'generously' into 'gen', where Snowball gives 'organ' and 'generous'.

Over-stemming merges unrelated words: Porter reduces both 'university' and 'universe' to 'univers', and 'organization' to 'organ'. Under-stemming misses related ones: irregular 'ran' stays 'ran' while 'running' becomes 'run'.

Stemming is fast and raises recall in search, since 'connected', 'connecting' and 'connection' all become 'connect', but it can lower precision and makes output hard to read, so measure its effect on your task.

key_points: Lemmatisation maps a word to its dictionary form, its lemma, using a vocabulary and morphological rules, so irregular forms work too: 'geese' becomes 'goose' and 'were' becomes 'be'.

NLTK's WordNetLemmatizer treats every word as a noun unless told otherwise: lemmatize('running') returns 'running' while lemmatize('running', pos='v') returns 'run', and lemmatize('was') returns 'wa', a classic mistake.

Get parts of speech from a tagger such as nltk.pos_tag, which needs nltk.download('averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng') in NLTK 3.9 and later, then map Penn Treebank tags to WordNet's: tags starting J to 'a', V to 'v', R to 'r' and everything else to 'n'.

Lemmas are real words and keep distinctions stemmers lose ('better' as an adjective becomes 'good'), but lemmatisers are slower, need tagging and only know the words in their dictionary. spaCy and Stanza lemmatise many languages inside their pipelines.

modules.summary: Write NLP code that scales and can be trusted: stream corpora with generators, compose small pure functions, choose data structures and algorithms for counting, and organise and test your code with pytest, ending with a tested bigram language model.

lessons.title: Iterators and generators for large corpora
objectives: Write generator functions that stream text a line or a token at a time
Avoid the single-pass pitfall of iterators
key_points: An iterable is anything a for loop can walk through; an iterator hands out one item at a time with next() and remembers its place, and once it's exhausted it stays empty.

A generator function contains yield: calling it returns a generator that runs lazily, only as far as the next yield, so a function that yields the tokens of each line of a file can stream a corpus of any size in little memory.

Generator expressions, such as (w.lower() for w in tokens), work like list comprehensions without building the list, and chain into pipelines: lines, then tokens, then filtered tokens, then a Counter.
Iterating a generator twice is a common bug: the second loop silently sees nothing. Build a list if you need several passes and it fits in memory, or call the generator function again.

itertools helps with streams: islice(stream, 10) takes the first ten items, chain.from_iterable() flattens a stream of token lists, and pairwise() (Python 3.10 and later) yields overlapping pairs, which are bigrams.

lessons.title: Functional programming for text
objectives: Use functions as values with map, filter, sorted and lambda
Write small pure functions that compose into a pipeline
key_points: Functions are values in Python: you can pass them as arguments, keep them in a list and return them, so a pipeline can be a list of steps applied in turn.
map(f, items) applies f to every item and filter(pred, items) keeps the items for which pred is true; both are lazy, and a comprehension often says the same thing more readably.
sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0])) sorts by count, highest first, and breaks ties alphabetically, so a report comes out in the same order on every run.
A pure function's result depends only on its arguments and it changes nothing outside itself; pure normalising and tokenising functions are easy to test and safe to reuse.

functools.partial fixes some of a function's arguments, so partial(re.sub, r'\s+', ' ') is a function that collapses the whitespace in any string it's given; functools.reduce folds a sequence into a single value.

lessons.title: Algorithm design for text: counting, bigrams and perplexity
objectives: Choose data structures that keep text algorithms fast
Build a bigram language model with add-one smoothing
Measure a language model with perplexity
key_points: Choose data structures by the operation you repeat: looking up a key in a dict or set takes about the same time however big it is, while searching a list takes longer the longer it gets, so count with a dict or Counter in a single pass.

A bigram language model estimates P(word | previous word) as count(previous, word) / count(previous). Padding each sentence with <s> and </s> lets it learn how sentences start and end, and a sentence's probability is the product of its bigram probabilities.
Add log probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities: a product of many small numbers underflows to zero in floating point, while a sum of logs stays well within range.

A bigram missing from the training data gets probability zero, which makes a whole test sentence impossible. Add-one (Laplace) smoothing adds 1 to every bigram count and the vocabulary size V to each denominator: (count(prev, w) + 1) / (count(prev) + V); add-k uses a smaller k.

Perplexity measures how well a model predicts unseen text: the exponential of the average negative log probability per predicted token, counting </s>. Lower is better, and it's only comparable between models with the same vocabulary and tokenisation.

Map test words never seen in training to an <UNK> token in the vocabulary, and tune k on held-out data, never the test set; add-one usually gives unseen bigrams too much probability, so a smaller k often does better.

lessons.title: Organising and testing NLP code
objectives: Structure an NLP script as importable functions with a command-line entry point
Write pytest tests for text-processing functions, including edge cases
key_points: Put reusable code in functions in a module, and call main() under if __name__ == '__main__':, so tests and other scripts can import the module without running it.
Docstrings and type hints, such as def tokenize(line: str) -> list[str]:, record what each function expects and returns; sys.argv or argparse turns command-line arguments into parameters.
pytest finds files named test_*.py and runs their test_ functions; each test runs your code on a small input whose answer you've worked out by hand and checks it with a plain assert.
Test the edge cases text throws at you: empty strings and blank lines, input that's only punctuation, contractions, accented and non-Latin characters, and words never seen in training.
Compare floating-point results with pytest.approx, as in assert p == pytest.approx(2 / 3), and use the tmp_path fixture to give a test its own temporary folder for files.

modules.title: Tokenisation, edit distance and regex in practice
modules.summary: Write regular expressions with groups and lookarounds, design tokenisers for messy text, compute edit distance to correct spelling, and see how subword tokenisers such as byte-pair encoding split words.

lessons.title: Regular expressions in practice: groups and lookarounds
objectives: Write regular expressions with character classes, quantifiers and groups
Use lookahead and lookbehind to match by context
key_points: Write patterns as raw strings, r'\d+', so backslashes reach the regex engine unchanged. re.findall returns every match, re.finditer yields match objects with positions, re.sub replaces and re.split splits.
The quantifiers *, + and {m,n} are greedy and match as much as they can; adding ? makes them lazy, so r'<.+?>' matches one HTML tag where r'<.+>' runs from the first '<' to the last '>' on the line.

Parentheses capture, and when a pattern has groups re.findall returns the groups instead of the whole match, a common surprise. (?:...) groups without capturing, and (?P<year>\d{4}) names a group that m.group('year') reads.

Lookarounds check what's beside a position without consuming it: (?=...) lookahead, (?!...) negative lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind and (?<!...) negative lookbehind. r'(?<=€)\d+' finds amounts after a euro sign without including the sign.

Python's re module needs lookbehinds of fixed width, so (?<=€|EUR )\d+ raises 'look-behind requires fixed-width pattern' while (?<=€)\d+|(?<=EUR )\d+ works. re.VERBOSE lets you spread a long pattern over several lines with comments.

lessons.title: Tokenisation strategies and tricky characters
objectives: Compare whitespace, rule-based and regular-expression tokenisers
Handle punctuation, contractions, numbers, URLs, hashtags and emoji deliberately
key_points: Every tokeniser makes decisions: whether "don't" is one token or two, whether 'e-mail' splits at the hyphen, whether '$4.50' or '20%' stays whole. Choose rules that suit the task, and apply the same ones to training data, test data and queries.

nltk.word_tokenize follows Penn Treebank conventions, so "Don't" becomes 'Do' and "n't", and it splits sentences first with the Punkt model, which needs nltk.download('punkt_tab') in NLTK 3.9 and later. It breaks URLs and email addresses into pieces.
Punkt sentence splitting knows about abbreviations, so 'Dr. Smith arrived at 3 p.m. He was late.' is split after 'p.m.' but not after 'Dr.', where splitting at every full stop gets both wrong.

A regular-expression tokeniser gives full control: list the specific patterns first (URLs, email addresses, money, numbers, words with inner hyphens or apostrophes) and a catch-all for single symbols last, because alternatives are tried left to right and the first that matches wins.

Social media text needs its own rules: NLTK's TweetTokenizer keeps hashtags, @mentions, URLs and emoji whole. Languages written without spaces, such as Chinese, Japanese and Thai, need dedicated word segmenters.

lessons.title: Minimum edit distance and spelling correction
objectives: Compute minimum edit distance with dynamic programming
Build a simple spelling corrector from edit distance and word frequencies
key_points: Minimum edit distance is the smallest number of edits (insertions, deletions and substitutions) that turns one string into another. With every edit costing 1, the Levenshtein distance, 'kitten' to 'sitting' is 3.

Dynamic programming fills a table D in which D[i][j] is the distance between the first i characters of the source and the first j of the target: D[i][0] = i, D[0][j] = j, and D[i][j] = min(D[i-1][j] + 1, D[i][j-1] + 1, D[i-1][j-1] + (0 if the characters match, else 1)).
The table takes time and memory proportional to the product of the two lengths; recording which choice won in each cell (a backpointer) recovers the alignment, the edits themselves.

Costs are a modelling choice: if a substitution costs 2, 'intention' to 'execution' is 8 instead of 5 (nltk.edit_distance(a, b, substitution_cost=2)). With transpositions=True, swapping two adjacent letters counts as one edit, so 'teh' is 1 from 'the' instead of 2.

A simple spelling corrector proposes known words within distance 1 or 2 and picks the most frequent. Allowing swaps matters: with Brown corpus counts, plain Levenshtein corrects 'teh' to 'ten' and 'recieve' to 'relieve', while counting transpositions gives 'the' and 'receive'.

lessons.title: Subword tokenisation: byte-pair encoding and its relatives
objectives: Explain why modern language models split words into subwords
Trace how byte-pair encoding learns and applies merges
key_points: A fixed word vocabulary can't cover every word, so new names, typos and rare inflected forms all become unknown. Subword tokenisers split rare words into frequent pieces while keeping common words whole, so any word can be represented.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) learns its vocabulary from a corpus: start from single characters plus an end-of-word marker, count adjacent symbol pairs across all words weighted by word frequency, merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and repeat for a chosen number of merges.

On the toy corpus low ×5, lower ×2, newest ×6 and widest ×3 the first merges are e+s, es+t and est+</w>. To tokenise new text BPE applies the learned merges in the same order, so the unseen word 'lowest' becomes 'low' + 'est</w>'.

The number of merges sets the vocabulary size: more merges give shorter token sequences but a bigger vocabulary to learn. BERT's WordPiece vocabulary has 30,522 entries and GPT-2's byte-level BPE 50,257.

The relatives differ in detail: WordPiece (BERT) picks the merge that most increases the likelihood of the training data and marks word-internal pieces with ##; SentencePiece's unigram model prunes a large vocabulary and treats the space as an ordinary symbol (▁); byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values, so no character is ever unknown.

project.title: Build a mini-corpus processing pipeline
project.brief: Kilbrack, a small harbour town, has sent you a raw mini-corpus: two months of community noticeboard posts, a page of ferry service updates in HTML, visitor reviews, and a held-out file of May notices. Build an end-to-end Python pipeline that loads every file (extracting the HTML page's text), normalises Unicode and typography, tokenises with your own regular-expression tokeniser, and extracts the emails, dates, euro prices and hashtags with named groups and lookarounds. Report frequency distributions, including a comparison of chosen words across the files with a ConditionalFreqDist. Then build a bigram language model on the training files: report the most probable bigrams with their probabilities, choose a smoothing value k on a development split of the training text, and measure perplexity on the held-out May file. Organise the code as a small, tested package with a command-line entry point, so the whole report comes from one command.

A pytest file with at least eight meaningful tests, including edge cases such as a decomposed accent, a curly apostrophe, an email address and an unseen word, all passing
The report: token and type counts before and after normalisation; the emails, dates, prices and hashtags found, with counts; the top 15 content words; and a table comparing chosen words across files
Bigram results: the 10 most frequent bigrams with their probabilities, development-set perplexity for at least three values of k, and held-out perplexity for the k you chose
